bands.label: Ages 6 to 11
bands.name: Build
bands.by: What this looks like by age 11
bands.title: Skill building and confidence
intro: Between 6 and 11, kids are in a powerful skill-building window, but the real goal isn't to cram in more academics. The most important outcomes at this stage are curiosity, confidence, and a love of learning. When kids believe "I can figure things out," they take on harder challenges, stick with them longer, and learn faster, in reading, writing, math, everything.

This is also when learning becomes meaningful. Kids start asking deeper questions and wanting to understand how the world works. So instead of chasing more content, aim for better learning: real books, real conversations, real problems, and projects with a purpose. Short, steady routines help, but the heart of this stage is building independence and competence without crushing motivation.

And yes, free play still matters at 6 to 11. Not because kids "need a break," but because play keeps training the skills that make learning easier: self-regulation, creativity, negotiation, and problem-solving. If you want strong thinkers later, protect play now.

Technology is part of childhood now, so the goal isn't fear or total avoidance. It's healthy, intentional use: a tool, not a default. The best rule is to create more than you consume. Kids this age do best with clear boundaries (when, where, how long), purpose first ("What are you going to make?"), coaching on safety, ads, and misinformation, and plenty of movement, outdoor time, and real responsibility.
focus: Read daily and talk about ideas
Math in real life: money, measurement, games, cooking
week: Read for 20 minutes (their choice), then a 30-second book trailer
Store game: a pretend shop with real prices, budgets, and change
Nature journal: walk outside, sketch one thing, write 3 observations
Building challenge: a bridge from household materials that holds a book
Cooking project: they pick a recipe, write the list, do the math to double it
Spot the trick: look at 3 ads together. What are they trying to make you feel or do?
Opinion battle cards: a low-stakes topic, 3 reasons and 1 counterpoint
Shadow tracking: mark a shadow at 10, 12, and 2. What happened?
Teach-back: they teach you something from this week in 2 minutes
Passion project: whatever they want to make, build, or research. No guidance
bands.weekend: Weekends are for day trips, family projects, board games, and doing nothing. A morning at the farmers' market teaches economics. A rainy afternoon with LEGO teaches engineering. A conversation at dinner teaches more than any worksheet.

pages.subtitle: Reading to understand
develop: Fluent reading: accuracy, pace, expression
Comprehension: main idea, details, inference, predictions
Comparing texts and noticing the author's purpose and bias (intro level)
Vocabulary growth through context
looks: Can summarize a chapter or article clearly in their own words
Can answer why and how questions with evidence from the text
Reads independently, for information and for enjoyment
ways: Book trailer: a 30 to 60 second pitch for a book, like a movie preview
Detective reading: highlight clues that show character traits or cause and effect
Choose your own ending: write or act out a new ending
Read and build: follow written instructions to build something or cook a recipe
Two-source challenge: read two short texts and list what agrees and what doesn't
Story walk: read outdoors, then teach it back while walking
pages.talk: If your kid reads below grade level, don't panic and don't drill. Find books they actually care about, even if they're "too easy." Volume and enjoyment build fluency faster than pressure.

pages.subtitle: Clear thinking on paper
develop: Strong sentences, then paragraphs, then multi-paragraph pieces
Narrative, informative, and opinion writing, with reasons and evidence
Planning, revising, editing (a simple checklist)
Writing for real purposes: emails, notes, instructions
looks: Writes organized paragraphs with a topic sentence and details
Can revise to improve clarity, not just fix spelling
Can write a short report or opinion with reasons and examples
ways: Comic to article: turn a comic story into a news report
How-to challenge: write instructions and test them on someone
Opinion battle cards: pick a topic, write 3 reasons and 1 counterpoint
Nature reporter: write a short field note outside
Postcards and emails: weekly messages to family and friends
Mini publishing: a booklet or zine with a cover, contents, and "issue #1"
pages.talk: Most kids hate writing because they've only been asked to write about things they don't care about. Let them write about what they love (a Minecraft strategy guide, a pet care manual, a comic series) and the skill transfers.

pages.subtitle: Number sense through real life
develop: Basic facts plus flexible strategies, not only memorization
Fractions and decimals, place value, estimation
Measurement, time, money, graphs and data
Word problems: modeling with drawings, tables, bar models
looks: Solves multi-step problems and explains their thinking
Uses fractions and decimals confidently in daily life
Reads charts and graphs and can say what they mean
ways: Store game: budget, discounts, tax, making change
Cooking math: scale a recipe up or down, fractions in action
Measurement scavenger hunt: estimate, then measure things outside
Data detective: track something for a week (steps, weather, birds) and graph it
Math games: card and dice games that build operations naturally
Build and calculate: design a fort or LEGO city and work out perimeter, area, scale
pages.talk: If your kid "hates math," they probably hate worksheets. A kid who plans a budget for a pretend store, scales a recipe, or figures out how many tiles fit in a room is doing real math and doesn't know it.

pages.subtitle: Claim, evidence, reasoning
develop: Asking better questions; telling fact from opinion
Cause and effect, patterns, analogies
Evidence habits: "How do you know?"
Learning from mistakes (debugging)
looks: Can support a claim with evidence and explain their reasoning
Can change their mind when new evidence appears
Can spot weak arguments ("that doesn't prove it")
ways: Mystery solver: work out "what happened?" from clues (pictures, objects, tracks)
Debate games: low-stakes topics ("best pet?") with evidence rules
Spot the trick: ads and posters. What are they trying to make you do?
Science mini-tests: predict, test, observe, explain
Logic puzzles and escape rooms: homemade clue hunts
Error hunter: find and fix mistakes in a messy solution together
pages.talk: The single most useful question you can ask your child at any age: "How do you know?" Not as a challenge. As genuine curiosity. That one question builds more critical thinking than any curriculum.

pages.subtitle: Search, safety, and first AI use
develop: Keyboarding and file skills: folders, naming, saving versions
Search skills: keywords, questions, comparing sources
First AI use: brainstorming, outlining, improving writing, always with checking
Digital safety: privacy, scams, respectful behavior online
looks: Can organize digital work (folders, file names, a simple routine)
Can tell when a source seems unreliable and look for confirmation
Can use AI as a helper and still produce their own thinking
ways: Source scavenger hunt: find 3 sources and rank them from most to least trustworthy
AI vs. human: ask AI a question, then check it with two trusted sources
Prompt practice: "make it shorter, clearer, for a younger kid"
Digital creation hour: slides, posters, a simple video. Make, don't consume
Keyboarding games: short daily challenges
Privacy sorting game: what's safe to share and what isn't?
pages.talk: The goal at this age isn't to keep AI away. It's to make sure your kid never trusts a confident answer without checking it. Do it together, out loud, the first few times, so checking becomes the habit.
library: AI Basics: Myths, Facts & Smart Rules

pages.subtitle: Speaking, listening, presenting
develop: Explaining their thinking clearly (math, reading, projects)
Listening and asking follow-up questions
Presentation skills: voice, structure, confidence
Giving and receiving feedback respectfully
looks: Can present a topic for 2 to 5 minutes with a clear structure
Can ask good questions and respond thoughtfully
Can handle feedback without shutting down
ways: Teach-back: your kid teaches you yesterday's learning in 2 minutes
Show and explain: bring an object and explain its story or science
Podcast minute: record a 60 to 90 second episode on a topic
Interview game: take turns being guest and host
Feedback ladder: "I liked... I wondered... What if...?"
Role-play: phone calls, ordering food, asking for help politely
pages.talk: Presentation skills feel like a "nice to have" until you realize that the kid who can explain their thinking clearly gets taken seriously by adults, peers, and eventually employers. Start small. A 2-minute teach-back at dinner is enough.

pages.subtitle: Feelings, friendships, repair
develop: Naming emotions beyond "fine" and "mad" (disappointed, overwhelmed, jealous, proud)
Reading social cues: tone, facial expressions, body language
Navigating friendships: exclusion, disagreements, shifting groups
Repairing relationships after conflict without an adult scripting every word
looks: Can name what they're feeling and why, most of the time
Can tell "I'm angry" apart from "I'm actually embarrassed" or "I'm actually hurt"
Can repair a friendship after a conflict, not just avoid the person
Can handle losing, being wrong, or not getting picked without it ruining the day
Notices when someone else is struggling and responds genuinely
ways: Rose, bud, thorn at dinner: the best part, something to look forward to, the hardest part
Feelings spotter: pause a movie or book. What is that character actually feeling?
Friendship role-play: practice tricky moments out loud. "What would you say if someone left you out?"
The after conversation: revisit a hard moment later. "What happened? What would you try next time?"
pages.talk: This is the skill that gets skipped because it doesn't look like "learning." But a kid who can read a room, repair a friendship, and bounce back from a bad day is better prepared for life than a kid who can ace a test but falls apart when things go sideways.

pages.subtitle: Routines, focus, independence
develop: Planning a day or week (simple checklists)
Focus stamina: short blocks that grow over time
Staying regulated when things get hard
Growth mindset: effort, strategy, and feedback
looks: Can start tasks with less resistance
Can work in focused blocks (15 to 40 minutes, depending on the kid)
Can use coping tools when frustrated (a break, a reset, asking for help)
ways: Beat the timer: short 10 to 15 minute missions with a fun finish
Choice boards: kids pick the order (more say, less friction)
Goal tokens: earn tokens for habits, trade them for privileges
Routine songs: for transitions like mornings and cleanup
Challenge ladder: gradually harder tasks, celebrate the effort
Reflection: rose, bud, thorn about the day
pages.talk: A kid who "won't focus" often just has a task that's too long or too vague. Shrink it: one clear mission, a timer, a finish line. Focus grows from small wins, not from lectures.

pages.subtitle: Design, build, iterate
develop: Generating ideas and planning
Prototyping, testing, improving
Artistic expression and storytelling
Basic maker skills: crafts, simple tools, building
looks: Can complete multi-step projects and improve them after feedback
Can explain their design choices ("I did this because...")
Enjoys creating and sharing their work
ways: Inventor prompts: build something that solves a real problem at home
Design a game: rules, fairness, testing with others
Stop-motion: simple animation with toys
Build challenge: tallest tower, strongest bridge, waterproof shelter
Art and story mashup: make art, then write the story behind it
Mini business: make a product (cards, crafts) and sell it to family, with a budget
pages.talk: If the first version is bad, the project is working. The whole point of making things is learning what doesn't work. Resist the urge to help them skip the messy part.
library: Create a Creature + Build Its Habitat

pages.subtitle: Values in action
develop: Responsibility, honesty, respect, empathy
A community mindset: helping, contributing
Kindness online, consent, boundaries
Cultural curiosity and openness
looks: Can take responsibility for mistakes and make it right
Shows empathy and can resolve conflicts with words
Understands basic digital citizenship and follows the rules
ways: Kindness missions: weekly secret helpful acts
Community project: a clean-up walk, a donation drive, helping a neighbour
Perspective play: "how would they feel?" role-play
Story ethics: talk about the choices characters make in books and movies
House rules council: a family meeting where kids propose solutions
Cultural cooking nights: food, geography, and respect
pages.talk: Kids learn character from what they see you do far more than from what you tell them. Let them see you apologize, help a neighbour, and admit when you got something wrong.

pages.subtitle: Practical competence
develop: Cooking basics, hygiene routines, organization
Money basics: earning, saving, spending, giving
Time management: packing, being ready, planning
Safety: simple first aid awareness, street safety, asking for help
looks: Can pack a bag and manage their belongings
Can make simple meals and snacks and clean up
Understands basic money decisions and can save toward a goal
ways: Meal planner challenge: pick a meal, budget it, write the shopping list
Allowance jars: save, spend, give, with a goal to track
Laundry math: sorting, timing, folding races
Home safety hunt: find the flashlight, the first aid kit, the exits
Grown-up role-play: appointments, schedules, polite phone calls
Travel planner: plan a day trip with a budget, a map, and timing
pages.talk: A 10-year-old who can cook a simple meal, do their own laundry, and manage a small amount of money is not "growing up too fast." They're building the confidence that comes from being genuinely useful.

pages.subtitle: Daily movement and outdoor confidence
develop: A daily movement habit, not just organized sports
Outdoor confidence: comfort in different weather, terrain, and free time outside
Physical challenge: trying hard things with their body, not just their brain
Body awareness: noticing tense, tired, or wired before it becomes a problem
Finding the kind of activity they actually enjoy
looks: Moves their body daily without being told (a habit, not just compliance)
Can try a new physical activity without refusing because it's hard or unfamiliar
Spends time outside comfortably and independently, even in imperfect weather
Has at least one physical activity they chose themselves
ways: Weekly movement challenge: how many push-ups by Friday? Can you climb that tree? Track it together
Outdoor skills: fire safety basics, knot tying, shelter building, trail navigation
Body check-in: "How does your body feel right now? Tight? Tired? Buzzy?"
Movement menu: biking, climbing, swimming, dancing, hiking, skateboarding, yoga. Help them find their thing, not yours
Build something heavy: a fort, a garden bed, a rock wall, a creek dam. Physical work with a visible result
pages.talk: Kids who move every day focus better, sleep better, and handle big feelings better. You don't need a sport or a schedule. You need a door to the outside and the patience to let them get a little cold, muddy, and tired.

bands.label: Ages 11 to 14+
bands.name: Apply
bands.title: Real-world application
intro: Adolescence is when learning stops being about "covering material" and starts being about who your kid is becoming. Confidence can skyrocket or motivation can quietly fade, depending on whether learning feels meaningful. The most important outcomes now are curiosity, identity, judgment, and independence: thinking clearly, communicating well, managing themselves, and making good decisions in a world that's changing fast.

At this age, your kid is ready for real responsibility and real work, not more busywork. They learn best when their skills go into something that matters: building a project, solving a real problem, creating something useful, contributing to family or community, and seeing the impact of their effort. That's why this section is about application: reading to understand the world, writing to persuade, math to make decisions, and critical thinking to tell what's true from what's noise.

Technology matters more than ever. Preteens and teens don't just need screen limits, they need digital judgment. Technology and AI should be tools for creating, organizing, and learning, not a default escape. A strong approach: purpose first ("What am I here to do?"), create more than you consume, and verify anything that shapes beliefs or decisions. It's also the perfect age for practical digital skills: organization, research habits, privacy, and spotting manipulation and deepfakes.

And while life gets busier, play still matters. It just evolves. Teens still need unstructured time to explore interests, move, socialize, and decompress. That breathing room protects mental health and creativity and keeps learning from turning into constant pressure. Structure helps, but meaning and balance are essential.
focus: One real-world project at a time: ship it, reflect, improve
Life skills and health habits that build independence
week: Read and discuss a news article or chapter: what's the author's argument? Do you agree?
Budget challenge: plan this week's family dinners within a set budget
Research mini-paper: one question, 3 sources, a short conclusion
Interview someone with an interesting job: 5 questions prepared in advance
AI and verification: ask an AI tool a factual question, then check it with 2 real sources
Passion project block: 60 to 90 minutes of deep focus, no interruptions
Presentation prep: a 3-minute talk on something they learned this month
Fix it or build it: a simple repair or something useful
Weekly reflection: rose, bud, thorn. What went well? What was hard?
Contribution: help a neighbour, plan a small donation drive, or write to the local council
bands.weekend: By this age, weekends should have stretches of real independence. Let them plan an outing. Let them cook a meal start to finish. Let them get bored and figure it out. The goal isn't to fill their time. It's to trust them with it.

pages.subtitle: Literacy and media fluency
develop: Deep comprehension: summarize, infer, analyze themes and arguments
Media literacy: bias, persuasion, misinformation, the incentives behind content
Strong vocabulary and precise language
Reading to learn: research, not just stories
looks: Can explain and critique an argument using evidence
Can compare sources and tell reliable from questionable
Can learn something from reading and teach it back
ways: Bias detective: compare how 3 sources cover the same topic
Article to brief: a one-page summary with key points and what they mean
Debate at home: take a side, argue it, then argue the opposite
Book to podcast: record a short review with quotes and takeaways
Incentives map: who benefits from this message, and why?
Teach-back workshop: present a topic to the family with visuals
pages.talk: At this age, the biggest literacy threat isn't that your kid can't read well. It's that they'll believe everything they read without asking who wrote it and why. Media literacy is reading for the real world.
library: Algorithm Awareness: Why Am I Seeing This?

pages.subtitle: Clarity, persuasion, structure
develop: Multi-paragraph essays and structured reports
Persuasive writing with counterarguments
Research writing: notes, citations, synthesis
Practical writing: emails, proposals, instructions
looks: Writes clearly with strong structure and transitions
Can revise for logic and clarity, not just spelling
Can write a convincing argument with evidence and a fair counterpoint
ways: Write a proposal: pitch a project with a budget, timeline, and benefits
Newsletter or blog: publish weekly for a real reader
How-to guide: write one and test it on someone else
Letter to a decision-maker: a real issue, a real ask
Research mini-paper: one question, 3 sources, citations, a conclusion
Portfolio page: their best writing with reflection notes
pages.talk: The ability to write a clear, persuasive email will matter more in your child's career than any essay they write in school. Give them real audiences to write for, not just you.

pages.subtitle: Math for decisions
develop: Ratios, percent, probability, and algebra thinking in context
Data literacy: charts, averages, misleading graphs
Personal finance: budgeting, compound interest, trade-offs
Modeling: turning real problems into numbers and decisions
looks: Uses math to make choices, not just solve exercises
Can interpret data and challenge misleading statistics
Understands basic finance and can budget independently
ways: Budget challenge: plan a month of spending with a savings goal
Price comparison lab: cost per unit, subscriptions vs. one-time, real value
Data project: track something (fitness, weather, expenses) and analyze the trend
Investing simulator: compare scenarios (risk, time, compounding)
Graph truth test: find misleading graphs and redesign them honestly
Trip planner math: routes, time, cost, a backup plan
pages.talk: The question that makes teen math click: "Is this a good deal?" Phone plans, subscriptions, a first paycheque. Real money turns percentages and averages into something they actually care about.

pages.subtitle: Judgment and logic
develop: Claim, evidence, reasoning at a higher level
Scientific thinking: variables, correlation vs. causation
Systems thinking: feedback loops, knock-on effects
Intellectual humility: updating beliefs
looks: Can argue from evidence and admit uncertainty honestly
Can spot common reasoning errors and weak proof
Can change conclusions when better information appears
ways: Myth-busting investigation: test a claim with sources and an experiment
Correlation trap hunt: find examples and explain why they mislead
Decision journal: decisions, predictions, results, lessons learned
Fallacy scavenger hunt: label the tactics in ads and social posts
Mini science study: design a test, collect data, share results
Systems map: map a real system (sleep, money, habits) and improve it
pages.talk: Teens who've practiced saying "I was wrong about that" without shame are rare and incredibly well-equipped for adulthood. Model it yourself first.

pages.subtitle: Prompting, verification, ethics
develop: Prompting as a skill: goal, constraints, examples, then iterate
Verification: cross-check sources, catch AI mistakes, cite evidence
Ethics: plagiarism, deepfakes, privacy, digital footprint
Digital organization: files, notes, workflows, versions
looks: Uses AI to amplify their thinking without outsourcing it
Verifies important claims with reliable sources
Understands privacy basics and makes safe choices online
ways: AI research workflow: question, AI outline, source checks, final report
Prompt portfolio: keep their best prompts and what worked
Deepfake awareness: build a "how to verify" checklist for the family
Fact-check challenge: take a viral claim and verify it end to end
Digital reset: build a clean folder and notes system, and keep it up
Ethics debate: AI at school and work. Write a personal policy
pages.talk: Banning AI from your teen's life is like banning calculators in the 1990s. The skill isn't avoidance, it's judgment. Teach them to use it without outsourcing their thinking.

pages.subtitle: Presenting, negotiating, collaborating
develop: Presentations with structure and confidence
Active listening and asking strong questions
Negotiation and conflict resolution
Collaboration: roles, deadlines, accountability
looks: Can present for 5 to 10 minutes with clear points and visuals
Can run a meeting or lead a small group project
Can handle disagreement respectfully and productively
ways: Host a family meeting: agenda, timekeeping, decisions, follow-ups
Interview project: interview 3 people and pull out what they learned
Presentation series: 4 mini-talks over a month (they improve fast)
Team build: plan and run a group event or outing
Feedback practice: what worked, what to improve, next step
Speaking challenge: record a talk, review it, improve it weekly
pages.talk: Teens get better at speaking by doing it in front of real people, not by reading about it. A family meeting they run, a call they make themselves, a talk for younger kids. Low stakes, real audience, every week.

pages.subtitle: Self-awareness and hard conversations
develop: Knowing what they feel before they react, even under pressure
Navigating complex social dynamics: shifting groups, gossip, social media drama
Hard conversations: disagreeing, saying no, setting boundaries without blowing things up
An identity separate from peer approval ("who am I when nobody's watching?")
Handling comparison and the gap between social media and real life
looks: Can sit with an uncomfortable emotion without reacting or numbing it right away
Can disagree with a friend and still be friends after
Can recognize when social media is affecting their mood, and step back
Can ask for help when something feels too big to handle alone
ways: Social media audit: track screen time and mood for a week. Change one thing
Hard conversation practice: script a real low-stakes situation, role-play it, then do it
Relationship map: who do they feel most themselves around? Who drains them?
Identity inventory: what do they actually like, vs. like because friends do? List 5 things that are theirs
Conflict replay: after a real argument, walk through what triggered it and what they'd do differently
pages.talk: This is the age when emotional intelligence either develops or gets buried under peer pressure and phone habits. A teen who can say "I'm actually hurt by what happened" instead of ghosting someone is rare. That skill doesn't happen by accident.

pages.subtitle: Planning, focus, follow-through
develop: Planning and prioritizing: a calendar and a weekly review
Focus skills: deep work blocks, managing distractions
Stress management and staying regulated
Healthy habits: sleep, movement, nutrition basics
looks: Can plan a multi-week project and follow through
Can manage distractions and work independently more often
Can recover from setbacks without spiraling
ways: 4-week goal sprint: set a goal, track habits, review results
Weekly planning ritual: a Sunday plan plus a daily 5-minute check-in
Focus experiment: test strategies (music or not, timers, phone rules)
Movement plan: measurable goals and reflection
Meal plan challenge: plan, shop, and cook 2 or 3 meals a week
Stress toolkit: build and practice a personal reset routine
pages.talk: If your teen can't focus, check their sleep and phone habits before assuming it's a motivation problem. Most focus issues at this age are environment issues, not character issues.

pages.subtitle: From idea to finished product
develop: Idea, prototype, feedback, iterate
Design thinking: user needs, constraints, improvement
Basic business thinking: value, cost, pricing, marketing
Creative expression in any medium
looks: Can take an idea and turn it into a finished product or service
Can gather feedback and improve without taking it personally
Understands value creation and basic money realities
ways: Micro-business: a product or service, pricing, simple marketing, review the results
Build a resource: a guide, template, or tutorial others can use
Video or blog series: teach something weekly with a content plan
Design challenge: redesign a frustrating household process
Portfolio: their best projects, with reflections
Community solution: spot a local problem and propose a fix
pages.talk: A teen who starts a small business (even one that fails) learns more about value, marketing, feedback, and resilience in a month than most adults learn in a year. Don't wait until they're "ready." They're ready now.

pages.subtitle: Ethics and contribution
develop: Values: honesty, responsibility, courage, respect
Digital citizenship: tone, consent, online footprint
Community contribution and service
Cultural awareness and empathy
looks: Takes responsibility and repairs harm when needed
Can discuss ethical dilemmas thoughtfully
Contributes to family and community in consistent ways
ways: Service project: volunteer, or start a community initiative
Ethics journal: a weekly reflection on choices, values, and impact
Digital footprint audit: review their online presence and set boundaries
Cultural deep dive: study a culture respectfully and share what they learned
Mentor role: teach a younger kid a skill every week
Community interview: find out what neighbours need most
pages.talk: Teens want to matter. Give them a real problem in their own community and real responsibility for fixing it, and you'll see a kind of motivation no assignment ever creates.
library: What Would You Do? Decision Lab

pages.subtitle: Practical independence
develop: Cooking, cleaning, laundry, basic home maintenance
Money: budgeting, saving, banking basics
Time: planning, being on time, travel readiness
Safety: first aid basics, situational awareness, asking for help
looks: Handles basic daily tasks with minimal reminders
Can manage a simple budget and make thoughtful purchases
Can plan a day on their own: schedule, transport, supplies
ways: Run the household for a day: meals, chores, timing, the whole thing
Personal finance system: track spending for a month and improve it
Cookbook build: 10 go-to meals with shopping lists
Fix-it basics: learn 5 simple repairs (sew a button, unclog a drain, patch a bike tire)
Emergency plan: contacts, kits, routines, meeting points
Solo day planner: plan an outing end to end (budget, timing, safety)
pages.talk: The test for this section: could your teen handle 48 hours on their own? Not perfectly, but safely and competently. If not, that's your priority list.

pages.subtitle: Owning their body
develop: Movement habits that happen because they want to, not because you scheduled it
Physical challenge and risk: pushing limits safely, learning what their body can do
Endurance and grit: finishing hard things, not just starting them
Outdoor independence: planning and doing physical adventures on their own
Respecting their changing body without obsessing over appearance
looks: Has a movement routine that doesn't depend on a parent organizing it
Regularly chooses to do something physically hard
Can push through discomfort (cold, tired, sore) without quitting right away
Can plan a physical outing (hike, bike trip, climbing day) with gear, route, and safety
ways: Fitness experiment: a 4-week movement plan. Track energy, mood, and sleep, not just performance
The big challenge: they plan something that stretches them. A long hike, a bike trip, a cold-water swim
Try three: 3 new kinds of physical activity in one month. What surprised them?
Outdoor overnight: a camping trip or backyard night out. They handle gear, food, and setup
Teach a younger kid: a sibling or neighbour learns a physical skill from them
pages.talk: Teens who have their own way of moving, one they picked, keep it as adults. Your job now is less coaching and more getting out of the way: trust them with the plan, the gear, and the hard parts.

welcome: If you've ever wondered, "Am I actually preparing my kid for real life, or just keeping them busy?" this guide is for you.

It's a practical map of the skills that matter most for kids to thrive, not just in school but in life. Kids need more than academics. They need strong foundations like self-regulation, communication, problem-solving, digital judgment, creativity, and real-world capability.

One belief sits behind every page: these skills are built by doing, not by studying. At the kitchen table, in the backyard, at the grocery store, on a trail, or in a new country. You don't need a perfect setup to raise a capable kid. You need the right priorities, a flexible plan, and a way to notice progress.
agesNote: The two age bands (6 to 11 and 11 to 14+) are flexible on purpose. Kids don't develop on the same timeline. Some master skills early, others later, and many are ahead in one area and behind in another. That's normal. Use the bands as chapters, not deadlines. If your kid is neurodivergent or develops differently, treat this as a menu of priorities, not a fixed path.
checkNote: You'll see checkboxes under each area's milestones. They're there so you can mark what your kid already does, not a to-do list to feel behind on. Most parents are surprised by how much they're already getting right.
disclaimer: This guide is for general planning. If you have concerns about your child's development or learning, talk to a qualified professional.

closing: Everything in this map is building toward one thing: a young person who can think for themselves, solve real problems, talk to people, and handle life when you're not standing next to them anymore. Not perfect skills. Not checked boxes. A person who's ready.

That doesn't come from covering every page. It comes from small, steady things. The conversations at dinner. The projects that fall apart and get rebuilt. The moments where they struggle and you don't rescue them. The days where nothing looks like school but everything looks like learning.

Pick 2 or 3 areas that matter most right now. Focus there. Let the rest wait. This is a map, not a checklist, and you were never meant to do it all at once. If you ever feel lost, go back to the three "Focus over formality" habits for your kid's age. Those three things are always enough.
